sources.news_title: Troy Jackson wins Maine Democratic Senate nomination, omits mention of Israel, AIPAC
sources.text:
Troy Jackson accepted the Democratic nomination for Maine’s US Senate race on Saturday with no mention of Israel, sidestepping an issue that has become a focal point for many Maine Jews as they assess the party’s new standard-bearer.
Jackson secured the nomination in a landslide 566 to 5 vote by delegates at the nominating convention. Saundra Pelletier, the only remaining challenger after the rest of the field dropped out in the days leading up to the gathering, picked up the handful of votes that didn’t go to the winner.
While Jackson took several shots during his acceptance address at Sen. Susan Collins, the incumbent Republican he will now face in the general election, it was Pelletier who used her remarks to specifically malign Collins’ voting record on Israel.
“She voted to increase federal funding in defensive arms for Iran, and did not vote to take moderate measures to hold Netanyahu accountable,” Pelletier said, receiving a chorus from the crowd.
The victory for Jackson came after the state’s former Democratic nominee, Graham Platner, a staunch Israel critic, left the race earlier this month amid a sexual assault allegation, which he has denied. The resulting scramble to replace him upended the Democratic primary and prompted fresh scrutiny from Jewish Mainers of Jackson’s recent evolution on Israel.
Jackson, a former state lawmaker and union advocate, had previously said little publicly about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict during his two-decade career in state legislature. However, during the race to replace Platner, he has embraced the term “genocide” to describe Israel’s war in Gaza and called for an end to US military aid to Israel on his campaign website, both positions championed by Platner before his exit. Jackson also has said he wouldn’t accept any funding from AIPAC.
Jackson omits mention of Israel, emphasizes Medicare, union, abortion rights
But on Saturday, as a sea of supporters sporting his campaign’s blue and yellow “Troy Jackson” t-shirts cheered their new nominee, Jackson omitted any mention of Israel from his remarks. Instead, Jackson reaffirmed his commitments to passing Medicare for all, supporting union rights, and restoring abortion rights nationwide, among other issues.
During his address following the decisive victory, Jackson also offered a message to Maine voters who remain on the fence:
“Whether you supported me from the beginning, supported another candidate, or are still deciding what you think of this fifth-generation logger from Allagash,” Jackson said. “I’ve always known this, that your trust has to be earned, and so I want you to hear this directly from me. There is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement, and I will spend every day, now through November, earning that trust because today we turn the page.”
Amy Fried, a professor emerita of political science at the University of Maine who attended Saturday’s conference as an alternate delegate but did not cast a ballot, said that while she believed Jackson had addressed Israel in the lead-up to Saturday because “a lot of people are interested in the topic,” his speech reflected the issues he had been “concerned about his whole political career.”
“Obviously, he’d have to take votes on foreign policy and funding when he’s in the Senate,” Fried said. “But I think that his main interest is always in issues that have to do with housing and healthcare, you know, all of the matters that are sort of more day-to-day kitchen table issues.”
While Jackson avoided revisiting his recent stances on Israel, which have raised concern among some Jewish voters in Maine, about a dozen pro-Palestinian protesters rallied outside the convention hall in support of his candidacy.
“It’s a really positive step that you have nominated Troy Jackson,” one protester shouted through a megaphone. “I think he’s going to be a strong voice for the kind of values that I believe in and the people of Palestine, the children of Iran, and all the other places the US bombed.”
Jewish delegate excited for Jackson's candidacy
Ronna Lugosch, a 71-year-old Jewish grandmother and delegate from Round Pond, Maine, said that she was “more excited now than I was before” about Jackson’s candidacy.
Lugosch, who supports Jackson’s stances on Israel, said she hadn’t noticed he had left the topic out of his remarks. “Unfortunately, it’s a sensitive topic, so that’s my guess that maybe he didn’t bring that up because it was just too much,” Lugosch said. “You know, he was being careful.”
Still, Lugosch said that she was “really impressed with all his comments about working people and organizing.”
“I’m going to campaign for him because we need to get rid of Susan Collins,” Lugosch said. “Before it was more of a sort of a defensive stance, but now I’m supportive, and so I feel better about going out into the community.”

sources.news_title: Maine Dems Declare Troy Jackson Winner of Convention for Sen. Primary
sources.text:
Maine Democrats formally declared Troy Jackson the winner of the Maine Democrat Party’s U.S. Senate Nominating Convention, meaning he will formally replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner in the race against incumbent Rep. Susan Collins (R-ME).
The Maine Democrat Party announced that Jackson secured the nomination at this weekend’s convention, receiving support from 566 delegates across the state.
“Congratulations to Troy Jackson on earning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate,” Maine Democratic Party Chair Charlie Dingman said in a statement.
“Maine Democrats engaged in this tightly scheduled nomination process with energy and enthusiasm. Tens of thousands of Democrats participated in selecting delegates, and today our delegates chose our nominee in a process that was open, representative, and transparent,” Dingman continued, asserting that Maine Democrats are now “united to support our nominee and focus on what matters most: defeating Susan Collins this November.”
He added, “Mainers are looking for a senator who will fight for working families, lower costs, protect our freedoms, and stand up for Maine. We’re excited to get to work to elect Troy Jackson and build a stronger future for our state.”
Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, was widely anticipated to win the convention, as the majority of delegates pledged to back him over his qualifying contenders, which included David Costello, Dan Kleban, and Saundra Pelletier. Notably, candidate Ashley Webb – the self-described transgender intersex individual who made waves for once claiming that he got his monthly period through his rectum – apparently did not qualify for the convention.
Jackson is a controversial individual with a reputation of having a boiling temper. Earlier this month, the far-left group Progressive Victory unveiled a troubling allegation against Jackson, alleging that he “struck a female colleague with a bottle he threw at her” during a disagreement, corroborated by several witnesses. The Washington Post has also described Jackson as someone who “once angrily threw a water bottle in a meeting after he couldn’t persuade a lawmaker to vote his way.”
While some Democrats are confident in this change in candidates, others remain doubtful. According to NOTUS, Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI) laughed when asked if Jackson had a better chance of winning than Platner.
“Let’s just say that we have a candidate,” she said.

sources.news_title: Troy Jackson Wins Democratic Senate Nomination, Setting Up November Showdown with Susan Collins
sources.text:
Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson officially secured the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate on Sunday, capping off a fast-moving replacement process that began after Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew from the race earlier this month.
Meeting at the Cross Insurance Center in Bangor, Democratic delegates overwhelmingly selected Jackson as their nominee, giving him 566 votes to 5 votes for fellow candidate Saundra Pelletier. The decisive margin ended weeks of speculation over who would replace Platner on the November ballot and sets up a high-profile general election against six-term U.S. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).
Jackson accepted the nomination before an enthusiastic convention crowd, thanking delegates, campaign volunteers, union supporters, his family, and fellow Democratic candidates who entered what he described as an “extraordinary moment” for the party.
Throughout his acceptance speech, Jackson framed his campaign around organized labor and working-class voters, repeatedly drawing on his background as a fifth-generation logger from Allagash and recounting his leadership during protests by Maine loggers against Canadian timber companies. Jackson argued that the struggle of loggers decades ago mirrors the economic challenges facing working families today.
“We’re only made to feel powerless when we stand alone,” Jackson told delegates. “That’s why I entered public life.”
Jackson outlined an unapologetically progressive platform that includes Medicare for All, expanded union organizing rights, restoring abortion rights nationwide, building more affordable housing, protecting Social Security and Medicare, confronting corporate price gouging, and standing against President Donald Trump and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He also pledged to stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Maine’s LGBTQ community.
Much of Jackson’s speech focused on attacking Collins, accusing the longtime Republican senator of siding with corporate interests and wealthy donors over working families.
Jackson criticized Collins for voting with President Trump, supporting Supreme Court Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch, backing the 2017 federal tax reform law, and opposing a congressional stock trading ban. He also revived a familiar Democratic attack by noting Collins’ 1996 campaign pledge to serve only two Senate terms.
“Thirty years later, Susan Collins is still in Washington,” Jackson said. “Who has she served?”
Jackson closed by urging Democrats, independents, and Republicans to unite behind his campaign, arguing that his movement is “not from the left” and “not from the right,” but “from the bottom.”
Saturday’s vote formally concludes a nomination process that has generated criticism from some Maine voters across the political spectrum. Following Platner’s withdrawal after winning the Democratic primary, party leaders selected Jackson through a convention of delegates rather than a statewide election, as provided under Maine law for replacing a withdrawn nominee.
While Democratic leaders defended the process as the legally prescribed method for filling the vacancy, some Democrats, independents, and Republicans questioned whether rank-and-file voters were effectively disenfranchised after more than 156,000 Democratic primary ballots had already been cast for Platner. Others argued the compressed timeline and delegate-selection process limited participation by ordinary voters.
Jackson’s political evolution is also likely to become a focal point during the general election. Once known as one of the Legislature’s few openly pro-life Democrats and a more moderate voice from rural northern Maine, Jackson has increasingly aligned himself with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party in recent years. His Senate campaign embraces many of the same priorities championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, including Medicare for All, expanded labor organizing, and broad federal economic intervention, positions Republicans are expected to use to portray him as the party’s latest progressive standard-bearer.
With the Democratic nomination now settled, attention shifts to what is expected to be one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races. Collins will seek a seventh term while Jackson attempts to unite Democrats and attract enough independent voters to flip one of the few remaining Republican-held Senate seats in New England.
The delegate vote may have ended the Democratic Party’s nomination battle, but the campaign for one of Maine’s most consequential federal offices is only beginning.

sources.news_title: Dems get renewed hope of ending GOP senator’s near-30-year career
sources.text:
Maine Democrats on Saturday overwhelmingly nominated Troy Jackson, a former state Senate president and logger by trade, as their party’s nominee to challenge longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in November’s high-stakes US Senate election.
“Well, thank you, Maine,” Jackson, 58, said after securing the votes of 566 of 571 delegates during Saturday’s special Democratic convention at Cross Insurance Center in Bangor. “Today we turn the page, today this becomes a general election campaign, and today we win the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.”
“For nearly 30 years, Collins has told Maine that she is ‘concerned’,” Jackson said, referring to the 73-year-old incumbent’s go-to word when President Donald Trump and Republicans attack rights and justice. “She was concerned while she rubber-stamped Trump’s Medicaid cuts and gutted our healthcare.”
“She’s concerned when she cut taxes for corporations and the wealthy,” he continued. “Concerned when she confirmed justices who overturned Roe v. Wade. And really tragically, she was concerned when she gave [US Immigration and Customs Enforcement] billions to terrorize our neighbors and murder people in the streets with no accountability.”
“But concern does not lower the costs of groceries or gas,” Jackson said. “Concern does not keep our monitoring wards of rural hospitals like down in Lincoln County open. Concern does not restore all the rights that she’s taken away. Maine does not need another six years of concern. We need someone with courage. We need a fighter, and we need a senator who remembers exactly who sent them to Washington.”
“So if you’ve ever been ignored, underestimated, pushed around, or told that you have to wait your turn while the rich cut the line, I’m asking you to stand with us in this campaign,” he continued. “If you believe in your heart that healthcare is a right, stand with us. And if you believe that workers deserve power, stand with us. And if you believe our freedoms are worth defending, stand with us.”
“And if you believe that Maine deserves a senator who will fight like hell for working-class people, well, stand with us,” Jackson added. “We have a party to unite, we have a movement to build, and we have a senator to defeat.”
Jackson’s improbably rapid rise followed former Democratic nominee Graham Platner’s withdrawal from the race earlier this month amid allegations of sexual assault and abusive behavior. Supporters of Platner’s progressive platform warned at the time that they would not back a replacement candidate who did not share the same pro-worker, anti-war agenda.
While Collins spokeswoman Blake Kernen called Jackson a “low-energy version” of Platner, Maine Democrats decided the fifth-generation lumberjack fit the bill.
“The working class has been left behind and forgotten about,” Shelly Mountain, a former Aroostook County Democratic Committee chairwoman and Jackson delegate at the convention, told NBC News. “He is definitely working class and always—has always—been a champion for the working class.”
Progressive politicians, advocacy groups, and labor organizations cheered Jackson’s nomination, with Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) saying that “he’s ready to fight for working people and flip this seat.”
International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) president Brian Bryant said Saturday that “Troy Jackson knows firsthand what it means to work hard for a living and fight for a better future for working families.”
“Throughout his career, he has stood shoulder-to-shoulder with union members and working people, never backing down from a challenge when workers’ rights were on the line,” he added. “He represents the strength of a people-powered movement focused on fairness, opportunity, and economic justice. Troy has our full support as he heads to the general election.”

sources.news_title: Democrat delegates nominate Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate
sources.text:
BANGOR -- Hundreds of Democrat delegates gathered in Bangor today to nominate Troy Jackson as the party's Senate pick.
The clinch comes after primary winner Graham Platner withdrew his campaign earlier in the month. With just over three months left in the campaign season, Jackson says he feels confident to gain voter support by November, and to defeat incumbent Susan Collins.
"I'm not for the billionaire class, I'm for the everyday working class," Jackson shared. "I think people should vote for me because I'm going to fight for them. I don't care about the party system, I'll push back against Democrats. I have in the Maine legislature. I'll push back against Republicans. I mean, it's about the issues."
Some delegates say losing Platner was a tough blow, but they're putting their faith behind Jackson.
"Seeing what has occurred has been heartbreaking, but I don't believe Susan Collins is going to win this. I say that because Troy Jackson has inherited a lot of that infrastructure, we're seeing a lot more strength among unions and volunteers," stated Penobscot County delegate Tristin Friend. 
"It has definitely been an all eyes on Maine situation...if everyone is paying attention to a state that has a population that's a fifth of the size of the island of Manhattan, clearly this matters. Not just to people in the state but to people outside of Maine," added Penobscot County delegate Jordan Simpson. 
Jackson now has around 14 weeks to campaign before Mainers cast their ballots.
"It really is about the billionaires and the everyday working class people in this fight. I'm going to stand with the workers, the everyday people, every day of the week," Jackson said.

sources.news_title: ‘Somewhere between a highwire act and a moonlanding’: Maine Democrats chose Troy Jackson in unprecedented U.S. Senate nomination
sources.text:
Maine Democrats used an unfamiliar process to choose a familiar face as their replacement nominee for one of the most closely watched races in the country.
A group of nearly 600 Democrats nominated former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson to be their U.S. Senate nominee in Bangor on Saturday, ending an unprecedented scramble to replace former nominee Graham Platner on November’s ballot just days before a state deadline.
Jackson won 566 votes of the 571 cast by party delegates at the Cross Insurance Center, defeating lone remaining challenger Saundra Pelletier, a biopharmaceutical executive and political newcomer. Jackson will now face Republican incumbent Susan Collins in November.
“This is the absolute honor of my life to accept the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate,” Jackson told the crowd in a speech after the results were announced, taking aim at Collins and styling himself as a fighter for working Mainers against corporate interests and the wealthy.
“If you’ve ever been ignored, underestimated, pushed around or told you have to wait your turn while the rich cut the line, I’m asking you to stand with us in this campaign,” he said.
Jackson quickly emerged from an initially crowded field to become the frontrunner for the nomination after Platner, who handily won the party’s nomination in the June primary, dropped out of the race on July 10, after a Maine woman accused him of rape. (Platner has denied the allegation.) With no clear process in place to replace Platner, the state Democratic Party moved quickly to plan and execute a convention of delegates from around the state to choose a replacement before a July 27 deadline.
Maine Democratic Party chair Charlie Dingman told the crowd that he had been advised that what the party was trying to do was “somewhere between a highwire act and a moonlanding.”
After Platner dropped out of the race, several Maine Democrats threw their hat in the ring, including Dr. Nirav Shah and Shenna Bellows, who, like Jackson, had recently ended unsuccessful campaigns for the party’s gubernatorial nomination. But Jackson grew a large lead in supportive delegates ahead of the convention, prompting all candidates but Pelletier to withdraw. Jackson had the backing of Maine’s labor unions and was the gubernatorial candidate most politically aligned with Platner.
A fifth-generation logger from Allagash, Jackson got his start in politics helping to organize a three-week blockade of the U.S.-Canada border to protest the hiring of Canadian loggers by U.S. landowners. Jackson has more than two decades of experience in Maine politics, serving as the president of the Maine Senate from 2018 to 2024. Over the course of his career, he also developed a reputation for a fiery temper, which once resulted in him throwing a water bottle out of frustration during a meeting of lawmakers.
Former Maine state lawmaker Charlotte Warren delivered introductory remarks for Jackson on Saturday, describing how he became her “hero” after he delivered an impassioned speech advocating for working people in the state Legislature two decades ago.
“You never have to worry where Troy’s heart is because he wears it on his sleeve,” she said.
Jackson’s mother, Colleen McBreairty, an Aroostook County delegate, said she was overwhelmed by her son’s nomination. “Never in a million years did I expect this,” she said.
But McBreaity said Jackson had always stood up for others. In second grade, Jackson came home and informed his mother he was going to write to then-President Jimmy Carter to inform him that a disabled student in his class was not being treated properly.
“I wish I would have kept that letter,” she said.
Crowded field became a coronation
Just last week, there were still a dozen Democratic candidates in the race to replace Platner. But a commanding effort to organize a slate of supporting delegates at 16 county-level nominating meetings put Jackson in a strong position heading into this weekend. Though party rules stipulated that no delegates entered the convention bound to one particular candidate, Jackson’s performance in the county meetings made clear that he already had majority support before the votes were counted on Saturday.
Candidate after candidate dropped out of the race following those county meetings, with many putting their support behind Jackson on the way out, until only he and Pelletier remained. A group of quickly-scheduled debates and forums were canceled, and what had been shaping up to be an unpredictable convention became more like a Jackson coronation where the result was never much in doubt.
“I thought it was incredibly disappointing that all those candidates dropped out because some of them were really qualified,” Pelletier said Saturday before the convention got underway. “And everybody claimed it was for unity. It was for fear, period.”
The political newcomer, who like Collins is from the Aroostook County city of Caribou, was realistic about her chances ahead of the convention. But she felt it was important to stay in the race and make it clear that the delegates were free to make a choice on Saturday rather than being automatically pledged to one candidate.
“We don’t want kings in this country,” Pelletier said. “Why would we anoint a king in the state of Maine? What message does that send to the country about the decisions that Mainers make and the Democratic Party makes?”
Pelletier said after the convention that she would support Jackson in his bid to unseat Collins.
Former Democratic congressional candidate Jordan Wood had initially sought the Senate nomination after Platner dropped out of the race, but he withdrew his candidacy and supported Jackson in the days leading up to the convention. Wood said the state party met its goal of instituting a process that “voters trust is their will, not a backroom deal.”
“I think there’s definitely things to learn for next time,” Wood said. “But I think people are really unified behind [Jackson] today, and I think that’s all you could hope for.”
An unprecedented process
Platner’s withdrawal from the race earlier this month, after already winning the June 9 primary with a record number of more than 156,000 votes, jump-started a process unlike anything seen before in modern Maine political history. While candidate replacement is a common occurrence at the state legislative and county levels, the Maine secretary of state’s office was unaware in early July of a previous instance where a statewide or federal candidate needed to be replaced after the primary election.
The Maine Democratic Party not only entered this process without precedent but also without much guidance from state law. The statute governing candidate withdrawals and replacements defines the timeline but not much else, leaving it to the political parties to decide how to choose a replacement. So Democrats had little more than two weeks to stand up a new process and make sure it concluded before the Monday deadline to provide replacement nominee information to the secretary of state’s office.
While there were a host of options available to the state party, Maine Democrats settled on a hybrid approach that had caucus-like meetings at the county level select delegates for the statewide convention. Some Democrats raised concerns about inclusiveness and transparency in the process, including after the emergence of candidate slates and Jackson’s dominance at the county level. Voters and at least one former candidate also criticized the exclusion of unenrolled voters, who had been allowed to participate in the record-setting primary, along with the party’s decision not to use ranked-choice voting.
But those concerns from some Democrats were typically couched with an understanding that party leaders were working to create a new framework on an incredibly condensed timeline.
Androscoggin County delegate Kiernan Majerus-Collins, who was on Jackson’s slate and is currently running for a seat in the State House, wished that ranked-choice voting could have been incorporated into the replacement nomination process, and acknowledged that the way the slate process played out at the county level likely overrepresented the delegate support for Jackson compared with his overall support among the primary electorate.
But Majerus-Collins stressed that he felt the party got the process “85, 90 percent right” in a very tight window of time.
“I would say that the party could have used a proportional representation system to ensure that the delegate allocations more accurately reflected what the voters want,” Majerus-Collins said. “That being said, I don’t think the outcome would have been any different. And I don’t want to be overly critical for people who pulled off, frankly, a miracle with no time.”
An all-Aroostook general election
Saturday’s convention result sets up a general election battle between two candidates who both hail from Maine’s northernmost county.
“Susan Collins and I both come from Aroostook county,” Jackson told the crowd. “But that is where the similarities end.”
The former Maine Senate president now faces the challenge of unseating a five-term incumbent with a significant fundraising advantage. The network of committees supporting Collins had $22 million in the bank at the end of June, according to Federal Elections Commission data. Jackson was unable to roll over $156,000 remaining from his unsuccessful bid for governor and essentially had to start from scratch, although his campaign said last week that he raised $1 million before securing the nomination.
Unlike Collins, Jackson has never won a statewide race and has failed in his previous attempts to secure his party’s nomination for higher office. In 2014, he was trounced by Emily Cain in the Democratic primary for Maine’s second congressional seat by 40 points. Earlier this year, he came in third in his party’s gubernatorial primary behind winner Hannah Pingree and Nirav Shah. He also lost a 2023 selectboard election in his hometown while still serving in the Maine Senate.
But Collins is also facing what is likely the most challenging political environment since she was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996. A recent University of New Hampshire poll put her 3 points behind Jackson. But polls also had her lagging behind Democratic nominee Sara Gideon in 2020 before she pulled off a convincing victory. Last week, Collins described Jackson as a “Bernie-bro” to CNN.
“She’s hard to beat, but I do think there is change in the air,” said state Sen. Craig Hickman, D-Winthrop. “I think that our nominee can continue to mobilize not just the party but working class people of all backgrounds.”
Democrats were clear-eyed about Collins’ financial advantage but argued that beating her would require on-the-ground organizing, a skill that Jackson’s campaign demonstrated on a smaller scale in securing the nomination.
“A campaign that is going to run successfully against Susan Collins needs to be able to build an army that’s organized and disciplined and understands what to do very quickly,” said Portland city councilor and Cumberland County delegate Wes Pelletier. “Troy is very clearly able to do that.”
Loren Andrews, a Knox County delegate from Cushing who was on Jackson’s slate, was impressed with Jackson’s performance at the county level.
“As a Jackson supporter for years, the organization it took to win that thing is mind-boggling,” Andrews said before the delegate vote on Saturday. “It should make Republicans very nervous about what we’ll be able to organize in the fall.”

Troy Jackson: Policies, background, and controversies of Maine's new Democratic Senate nominee
Troy Jackson, a former logger and state lawmaker, is now the Democratic Senate nominee set to face Susan Collins in Maine.
Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson has been chosen as the Democratic nominee for the US Senate in Maine. He will face longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins in November after Democratic primary winner Graham Platner withdrew from the race following a sexual assault allegation, which he has denied.
Who is Troy Jackson?
Troy Jackson. who is 58, and a former Maine Senate president and fifth-generation logger from rural northern Maine. He first ran for office as a Republican in 2000, seeking a seat in Maine's House of Representatives, but lost. He won two years later running as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004 and eventually became Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024.
He came in third while running for governor in this year's Democratic primary, but had the backing of Graham Platner and Our Revolution, the political organization founded by Bernie Sanders. When Platner dropped out on July 10, several former governor candidates, including Jackson, jumped in to try to take his place. By July 19, most had dropped their bids, leaving Jackson as the clear favorite.
“When the people in power refuse to listen, you have to organize, you have to stand in solidarity, together. And you have to make them listen,” Jackson said during a speech at the last-minute nominating convention.
Asked by reporters about being called a "Bernie Bro," Jackson said, “I don't really care. What I am is a guy from northern Maine that's a logger.”
Troy Jackson's policies
Jackson has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He has also called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month.
He said he would attack Collins on what he described as her record of supporting tax cuts for the wealthy and failing to protect health care. Both Jackson and Collins are from northern Maine, where traditional industries such as potato farming and timber harvesting are vital to the economy. Both are expected to argue over the next few months that they are the right leader to protect those industries, along with lobster fishing and tourism.
Also Read: Who is Troy Jackson's partner, Lana Pelletier? All on Maine Democrat Senate nominee's family
Controversies around Troy Jackson
Jackson replaces Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary in June but withdrew from the race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault, which Platner has denied.
Republicans have linked Jackson to Platner and called him too extreme for Maine voters. Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are "clearly" in line with socialism, adding, “He's a Bernie Bro,” noting that Jackson ran Bernie Sanders' first presidential campaign in Maine.
Collins' campaign spokesperson, Shawn Roderick, said, “Troy Jackson will attempt to sell Mainers a multi-trillion dollar bill of goods based on rhetoric that will make everything sound free, but in reality would be paid for by middle and lower income workers.”
RNC spokesperson Kristen Cianci also called Jackson “a Platner apologist, a radical Bernie Bro, and a walking red flag displaying all the warning signs of the early days of the Platner campaign.”
Jackson told reporters Saturday that he has not been in touch with Platner and is building a new movement. He acknowledged the disappointment of Platner's supporters, saying, “I agree there are people that are still very frustrated and angry what happened. I understand that. All I'm trying to do is explain to them that his campaign was about the issues.”
Republicans have also launched an ad campaign against Jackson, accusing him of having a volatile temper. The Senate Leadership Fund, Republicans' super PAC, said it is committed to spending over $42 million against Jackson.

sources.text:
BANGOR — Maine Democrats had a little over two weeks to replace Graham Platner as their U.S. Senate nominee. They finished the job by noon on Saturday, formally nominating Troy Jackson at a convention lacking in suspense but replete with hallmarks of Maine’s topsy-turvy election year.
The gathering of some 600 delegates at the Cross Insurance Center capped off the party’s abbreviated process to pick a new challenger for Sen. Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent who became as much a focus of the convention as Jackson was. After Jackson, the Allagash logger and former Maine Senate president, swept county delegate-selection meetings last weekend, Democrats wasted no time in turning their attention to the general election just 101 days away.
“Today we turn the page,” Jackson, a union-backed populist in Platner’s mold who placed third in the Democratic gubernatorial primary last month, said in a speech drawing on his repeated themes about fighting for the working-class.
It was his second time speaking in as many hours. The first time, he presented himself as one of two remaining candidates for the delegates to choose from — and took nearly double his allotted five minutes. Delegates elected him, 566 votes to 5, according to state party chair Charlie Dingman.
“It’s mostly a formality,” Keith Newman, a Democratic State Committee member and automatic delegate from Washington County, said of Jackson’s nomination before the voting. Newman said the withdrawal of all of Jackson’s major rivals to replace Platner “was not something I expected.”
Formality though it was, the convention featured many of the characters and motifs that have defined the state’s high-stakes election season, compressed into a glassy lobby and anodyne ballroom.
A former Platner volunteer wore a Platner campaign T-shirt, as many Democrats clung to the energy he galvanized before dropping out amid the fallout from a rape allegation he denies.
Devon Murphy-Anderson, the state party executive director who became well known in the last month for late-night direct-to-camera video updates, flashed her all-access pass at an unaware volunteer to enter the convention hall.
“We did it with the world watching,” she later said from the stage, thanking the state’s Democrats for contributing to the nominating process.
An Indigenous land acknowledgment by Dingman, the party chair, turned into a call for greater Wabanaki tribal rights; Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat absent from the convention, vetoed a bill to that end in 2023 and saw her Senate bid roundly rejected by Democratic primary voters earlier this year.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee for Congress in Maine’s 2nd District, stood against the wall near the back of the room, near the press area. “It’ll be nice to have this over so we can put a little bit more of the public focus on our campaign,” Dunlap said.
On a morning of self-conscious party unity, at least among attendees, nothing — not even the adoption of a “credentials report” — was too small for rousing applause. Excitement showed especially at any mention of beating Collins, a five-term senator who fashions herself as an independent-minded moderate but who came under fire here for her voting record of aligning with President Donald Trump.
The crowd gave a polite reception to Jackson’s sole opponent at the convention, the little-known Caribou entrepreneur Saundra Pelletier, who joined in the attacks on Collins and distributed copies of a 16-page manifesto titled “WHAT I BELIEVE.”
“My superpower is reading the room,” Pelletier said, prompting murmurs in a convention hall destined not to embrace her as its torchbearer, after she was introduced by her brother Troy Pelletier.
At a very different event the night before, in a ballroom in Washington, D.C., Trump had his mind on Maine.
“They nominated a guy with a Nazi tattoo. But don’t worry, Democrats, word is that Platner’s replacement, he throws bottles at women, this guy throws bottles — this guy’s another lunatic, by the way. Although I think Platner might’ve done surprisingly well, because we’re in the age of Trump,” Trump said Friday at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner rescheduled after an assassination attempt derailed this year’s original one. (Platner has said he got the tattoo without knowing of its Nazi links.)
Saturday’s program in Bangor appeared to take account of recent reporting on Jackson’s intensity in the state Senate, including the water bottle incident. Charlotte Warren, a former state representative whose 2021 clash with Jackson in Augusta was described in a Washington Post article, introduced Jackson as “passionate.”
In his victory speech after the convention officially adjourned, Jackson framed his progressive priorities around a resource that Platner often cited on the stump and that Maine Democrats have in short supply: time.
“We’re losing what little time we have with our families,” Jackson, 58, said in a speech in which he at times stumbled over his words.
“I spend all my time trying to catch up for life lost with my kids,” he continued. “And I see it, you know, with people everywhere. You know, they made it so hard that we’re always chasing something to try and put it all together, and our families suffer.”
In just over three months, Jackson will appear on the ballot against Collins for the chance to spend the next six years shuttling to Washington, D.C.
After he left the stage, the delegates filed out of the convention hall, and some sang the union standard “Solidarity Forever.”

Graham Platner, the original nominee to run against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, dropped out over sexual misconduct allegations
The Democratic Party in Maine picked its new candidate for a key US Senate race on Saturday, after the original nominee was pressured to drop out over sexual misconduct allegations.
Delegates to a hastily organised nominating convention picked Troy Jackson, a former state senate president, to go up against Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
“Thank you, Maine. In 101 days, we will defeat Susan Collins and reclaim our Senate seat. Let’s get to work,” Jackson said on social media.
The move comes just over two weeks after the prior candidate, Graham Platner, dropped out.
A Marine veteran, oyster fisherman and political newcomer, Platner had earlier won the Democratic primary with an energetic, anti-establishment message that gained him national prominence.
He weathered earlier scandals, including one related to a Nazi-linked tattoo, but his support plummeted after a former partner publicly accused him of rape.

After becoming Maine’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee at a Bangor convention Saturday, Troy Jackson told reporters it has been weeks since he spoken with the man he’s replacing on the ballot: Graham Platner.
The oyster farmer’s populist campaign roused labor unions and progressives, many of them longtime Jackson supporters, before collapsing earlier this month after Politico reported that an ex-girlfriend alleged Platner had raped her.
Jackson, a former logger from Allagash, told reporters in a news conference Saturday that, “people are still angry about what happened” with Platner’s scandal-plagued campaign.
He said he had not yet spoken with Platner, once a strong ally who campaigned alongside Jackson during Jackson’s unsuccessful gubernatorial bid, since the Politico story broke. But he said that there wasn’t much daylight between his policy vision and Platner’s message, which galvanized many Democrats aiming to oust the five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins and retake control of the Senate.
“His campaign was about the issues,” Jackson said of Platner. “If you want Medicare for all … a fair taxation system …I’ve been fighting for that forever. We don’t have to lose that momentum.”
Jackson nodded to his lack of polish as a politician, even though he roused Democrats to their feet several times before nearly 600 delegates voted to name him the nominee.
“I’m not a show horse,” he said. “I’m a work horse.”
Collins has far more cash on hand and Republican groups are already investing tens of millions of dollars in what’s expected to be the fourth-most expensive Senate race in the country in terms of ad spending, which AdImpact projects could reach almost $400 million.
The Republican senator has painted Jackson as “socialist” and “Bernie bro,” referencing Jackson ally Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont.
“Today, in a process concocted by the Maine Democratic Party establishment, a 24-year Augusta insider was appointed to run for the Senate by fewer than three-tenths of one percent of its primary voters,” Shawn Roderick, a Collins campaign spokesman, said in a statement. “Troy Jackson will attempt to sell Mainers a multi-trillion dollar bill of goods based on rhetoric that will make everything sound free, but in reality would be paid for by middle and lower income workers.”
Jackson said Republican attempts to fight his spot on the ballot based on the Democrats’ nominating process amounted to “bogus claims.”
Asked about reports that he previously treated state lawmakers, particularly women, with abrasiveness and a temper, Jackson said the GOP was going “to say whatever they can because they’re scared they’re gonna lose this race.”
“I’ve fought with people on both sides,” he said. “I wear my heart on my sleeve, I have cried on the Senate floor. Anyone that I may have argued with who I may have went too far or gotten too passionate, I apologize. But … yeah, I am passionate.”
Asked if he has enough money to compete with Collins, he said with a laugh, “Not now, but I hope we get it.”
Jackson raised $1 million in his rapidly developing Senate bid, and he said many of the donations were for $12 after he joked that Collins had $12 million, and he only had $12.
He shrugged off comments about him being a socialist or “Bernie bro.”
“I don’t know what I am, I don’t really care,” he said. “What I am is a guy from northern Maine. People can call me anything they want … and they have.”

BANGOR, Maine – Troy Jackson accepted the Democratic nomination for Maine’s U.S. Senate race on Saturday with no mention of Israel, sidestepping an issue that has become a focal point for many Maine Jews as they assess the party’s new standard-bearer.
Jackson secured the nomination in a landslide 566 to 5 vote by delegates at the nominating convention. Saundra Pelletier, the only remaining challenger after the rest of the field dropped out in the days leading up to the gathering, picked up the handful of votes that didn’t go to the winner.
While Jackson took several shots during his acceptance address at Sen. Susan Collins, the incumbent Republican he will now face in the general election, it was Pelletier who used her remarks to specifically malign Collins’ voting record on Israel.
“She voted to increase federal funding in defensive arms for Iran, and did not vote to take moderate measures to hold Netanyahu accountable,” Pelletier said, receiving a chorus from the crowd.
The victory for Jackson came after the state’s former Democratic nominee, Graham Platner, a staunch Israel critic, left the race earlier this month amid a sexual assault allegation, which he has denied. The resulting scramble to replace him upended the Democratic primary and prompted fresh scrutiny from Jewish Mainers of Jackson’s recent evolution on Israel.
Jackson, a former state lawmaker and union advocate, had previously said little publicly about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict during his two-decade career in state legislature. However, during the race to replace Platner, he has embraced the term “genocide” to describe Israel’s war in Gaza and called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel on his campaign website, both positions championed by Platner before his exit. Jackson also has said he wouldn’t accept any funding from AIPAC.
But on Saturday, as a sea of supporters sporting his campaign’s blue and yellow “Troy Jackson” t-shirts cheered their new nominee, Jackson omitted any mention of Israel from his remarks. Instead, Jackson reaffirmed his commitments to passing Medicare for all, supporting union rights and restoring abortion rights nationwide, among other issues.
During his address following the decisive victory, Jackson also offered a message to Maine voters who remain on the fence:
“Whether you supported me from the beginning, supported another candidate, or are still deciding what you think of this fifth-generation logger from Allagash,” Jackson said. “I’ve always known this, that your trust has to be earned, and so I want you to hear this directly from me. There is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement, and I will spend every day, now through November, earning that trust because today we turn the page.”
Amy Fried, a professor emerita of political science at the University of Maine who attended Saturday’s conference as an alternate delegate but did not cast a ballot, said that while she believed Jackson had addressed Israel in the lead-up to Saturday because “a lot of people are interested in the topic,” his speech reflected the issues he had been “concerned about his whole political career.”
“Obviously, he’d have to take votes on foreign policy and funding when he’s in the Senate,” Fried said. “But I think that his main interest is always in issues that have to do with housing and healthcare, you know, all of the matters that are sort of more day-to-day kitchen table issues.”
While Jackson avoided revisiting his recent stances on Israel, which have raised concern among some Jewish voters in Maine, about a dozen pro-Palestinian protesters rallied outside the convention hall in support of his candidacy.
“It’s a really positive step that you have nominated Troy Jackson,” one protester shouted through a megaphone. “I think he’s going to be a strong voice for the kind of values that I believe in and the people of Palestine, the children of Iran, and all the other places the U.S. bombed.”
Ronna Lugosch, a 71-year-old Jewish grandmother and delegate from Round Pond, Maine, said that she was “more excited now than I was before” about Jackson’s candidacy.
Lugosch, who supports Jackson’s stances on Israel, said she hadn’t noticed he had left the topic out of his remarks. “Unfortunately, it’s a sensitive topic, so that’s my guess that maybe he didn’t bring that up because it was just too much,” Lugosch said. “You know, he was being careful.”
Still, Lugosch said that she was “really impressed with all his comments about working people and organizing.”
“I’m going to campaign for him because we need to get rid of Susan Collins,” Lugosch said. “Before it was more of a sort of a defensive stance, but now I’m supportive, and so I feel better about going out into the community.”

sources.news_title: Troy Jackson wins Democratic nomination for US Senate in Maine - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
BANGOR — Eighteen days after the collapse of Senate nominee Graham Platner‘s campaign amid credible accusations that Platner raped an ex-girlfriend, Maine Democrats on Saturday turned the page by nominating former state Senate President Troy Jackson to take on longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins this fall.
Jackson is a fifth-generation logger and union organizer, who led Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaign in the state and espouses the same ideological outlook as Platner. He backs Medicare for All and has an economic populist message on housing and wages.
“Today we turn the page,” said Jackson in a nomination acceptance speech after coming out to Noah Kahan’s song “Northern Attitude,” which a staffer said was Jackson’s idea. “Today this becomes a general election campaign, and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.”
In the days that followed Platner’s exit, more than a dozen Democrats jumped into what became a scramble primary of sorts. But Jackson so dominated the convention delegate process last weekend — capturing 91 percent of the elected delegates — that all of his major challengers dropped out immediately afterward. The fact that he had run unsuccessfully for governor in the June primary meant he had already had a network of supporters in all of the state’s 16 counties.
Thus, what was supposed to be one of the rare political conventions in the modern era that actually mattered instead became another fait accompli.
Jackson received 566 votes from the delegates who voted at the convention. Just one other candidate, Saundra Pelletier, a health care executive, challenged Jackson at the convention, but she received just 5 votes.
“It’s been crazy,” Jackson told reporters about the last few weeks leading to his nomination. “It’s been, you know, really something like I’ve never seen before, but, you know, I have been in politics a long time fighting for these issues.”
Jackson, 58, now enters one of the country’s most competitive and pivotal Senate races this November against Collins, 73.
Maine’s Senate race is key to Democratic hopes of taking control of the Senate for the remaining two years of President Trump’s term.
To pull that off, Democrats must hold three competitive Senate seats in Democratic hands in New Hampshire, Michigan, and Georgia. They must also flip four seats currently held by Republicans. Collins is the only Republican up for reelection this year in a state that Trump lost in 2024.
Polling has consistently shown the race effectively tied, with Collins and Jackson running within the margin of error.
A statement from a Collins spokesman, Shawn Roderick, said, “Senator Collins looks forward to waging a vigorous and issue-oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy’s angry sound bites and far-left ideology.”
The moment Jackson was announced as the nominee, a Super PAC affiliated with Collins announced a six-figure ad buy labeling Jackson as “worse than Platner.”
In a 10-minute speech ahead of the vote, Jackson cast himself as a working-class outsider despite years in Augusta, describing himself as a fifth-generation logger and union organizer from Allagash, the remote northern Maine town where he grew up.
“I am nothing special,” he told a crowd waving “Retire Susan” signs. “I didn’t get involved in politics because I wanted a title. I got involved because the people that I worked beside were getting screwed, and nobody, nobody in power, seemed to care about them.”
Jackson focused most of his remarks on Collins, whom he accused of standing up for billionaires over Mainers. Collins, meanwhile, has based her pitch for a sixth term on the idea that she is a political moderate with the Senate seniority to bring money back to the state.
The convention marks a pivot point for Maine elections this fall. Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee in the state’s open 2nd Congressional District, said in an interview that all the drama surrounding the Senate race has “taken all the attention away” from his race and others.
“It’ll be good to get beyond this so that we can all get to pulling the plow in the same direction,” Dunlap, the former state auditor, said.
There was no mention of Platner during the 2½-hour convention. That was despite the fact that he is credited with building the largest grassroots campaign in Maine history, one that received 72 percent of the vote in the June primary.
Less than three weeks earlier, Platner had been the Democratic Party’s rising star and one of the country’s most closely watched Senate candidates. By Saturday, it was as though he had vanished from Maine politics.
An hour before the convention began, there was little activity at Platner’s home in Sullivan, 40 miles away. The regular security presence was gone, only two cars were in the driveway, and a single kitchen light was on. In Ellsworth, all signage for his state headquarters had been removed, and the office was filled with cleaning supplies as it was prepared for a new tenant.
Even the general store at the end of Platner’s street had removed the sign advertising its sandwich special, “The Graham,” in honor of the former political phenomenon.
The deli clerk said they had run out of roast beef.
James Pindell is a Globe political reporter who reports and analyzes American politics, especially in New England.

sources.news_title: Maine Democrats nominate Troy Jackson to replace Platner in US Senate race
sources.text:
WASHINGTON - Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson on Saturday won the state Democratic Party's U.S. Senate nomination, formally ending a two-week scramble to replace Graham Platner on the ballot for November's midterm election. Platner withdrew on July 10 after sexual assault allegations were made against him. He denies the allegations.
The overwhelming majority of some 600 delegates at a party convention on Saturday in Bangor selected Jackson over Saundra Pelletier, the wealthy chief executive of a biopharmaceutical company.
Jackson will face Senator Susan Collins, a Republican who has held the seat since 1997, in the general election. Maine is seen as a key battleground state that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the Senate.
The Democratic nominee's speech before the vote on Saturday reflected his party's broader push to tie Republicans to cost-of-living issues that are expected to influence the outcome of the midterm elections.
"Working people are getting crushed in this country. ... Meanwhile, the billionaires and corporations rigging this economy keep getting richer and Susan Collins has done every damn thing that they ask for nearly 30 years," Jackson said.
A fifth-generation logger and former Republican from northern Maine, Jackson locked up the nomination last weekend, when his supporters dominated the state party's delegate selection process. Jackson's campaign said on Wednesday it had raised more than $1 million since he jumped into the truncated race earlier this month.
AFFORDABILITY LIKELY TO BE A KEY ISSUE IN RACE
Jackson's nomination kicked off a 101-day sprint to unseat Collins, who has used her seniority and perch as head of the Senate Appropriations Committee to steer resources to Maine. She is the only Republican up for reelection in a state that Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris won in 2024, making Maine a top flip opportunity for Democrats hoping to regain control of the chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump's administration.
Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, but winning Maine is crucial to both parties' midterm strategies. Jackson held a narrow lead over Collins among likely general election voters in a University of New Hampshire poll released this week.
Collins, a 73-year-old moderate with an $11 million war chest, won her 2020 race by nearly 9 percentage points, even as Maine voters backed Democrat Joe Biden over Trump by a similar margin. Harris, herself a replacement nominee after Biden abruptly withdrew from the 2024 campaign, carried Maine by about 7 percentage points. Experts say affordability, Trump's leadership and immigration are likely to be key issues in the general election.
Jackson has called for abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, an agency that has killed several people in high-profile incidents this year, including a 26-year-old Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13. Collins voted for $70 billion in immigration enforcement funding without ICE reforms last month but has called for a pause in the agency's traffic stops.
Trump has since said such stops must continue, describing them as one of the agency's most important and effective tools.
Social issues will also likely surface in the contest between Collins and Jackson. Jackson now supports abortion rights and same-sex marriage but opposed both in his state legislative career until his second Senate term in 2016.
His anti-abortion Senate voting record was raised in ads against him during his unsuccessful run in Maine's gubernatorial primary this year. The Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC that has pledged to spend at least $42 million in Maine, launched a six-figure ad campaign against Jackson on Saturday aimed at making an issue of an incident in which he flung a water bottle during a 2021 legislative session.
The Republicans' 30-second YouTube spot says Jackson has "anger issues" and "a history of conflicts with women," calling him "like Graham Platner but worse."
The Washington Post and the New York Times have reported that the incident involving the water bottle occurred as Jackson engaged in a heated argument with Heather Sanborn, a Democratic state senator at the time, over a bill to lower prescription-drug costs.
In an interview with the New York Times earlier this week, Jackson said he should not have thrown the bottle, adding, "I was passionate. Do I wish I've never yelled or anything like that? Sure."
(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill, David Ljunggren and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Cynthia Osterman and Paul Simao)

Republicans have called Jackson too extreme for Maine voters, and Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are “clearly” in line with socialism.

Both will make the case over the next few months that they are the right leader to protect those industries, along with lobster fishing and tourism.
Collins noted that Jackson ran U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ first presidential campaign in Maine, adding “He’s a Bernie Bro.”
Asked by reporters about that description, Jackson said, “I don’t really care. What I am is a guy from northern Maine that’s a logger.”
He said he would attack Collins on what he described as her record of supporting tax cuts for the wealthy and failing to protect health care.
Jackson needs to scramble to make up a fundraising gulf against the incumbent, who has been raising money for months. Federal filings show she has raised more than US$16-million so far. Jackson’s campaign this week said he raised more than US$1-million since jumping into the Senate race.
Democrats have a narrow path to take back the Senate in November and it’s highly unlikely they can do it without a win in Maine. In addition, they need victories in competitive races in North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, and they need to hang on to the seats they already have. That includes open Senate seats in Michigan and Minnesota, where Democratic incumbents are retiring.
Maine’s Democratic primary was one of the early contests where progressives took on establishment-backed Democrats. While Platner faced several controversies during his campaign, he easily outlasted Gov. Janet Mills, who was backed by Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer but dropped out before the June 9 primary.
Platner had backing from Sanders as well as Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. That support disintegrated after the sexual assault allegation early this month.
Republicans began making the case Saturday that Jackson is too close to Platner. Jackson is “a Platner apologist, a radical Bernie Bro, and a walking red flag displaying all the warning signs of the early days of the Platner campaign,” RNC spokesperson Kristen Cianci said in a statement.

The Maine Democratic Party scrambled to choose a new nominee after Platner, who sailed to victory in the Democratic primary in June, was accused by a former girlfriend of sexually assaulting her in 2021. Platner denies the allegation, but quit the race after key supporters called on him to withdraw.
Maine law gave the state party authority to choose a replacement and required a new nominee to be named by Monday – 101 days before the Nov. 3 election.
Maine Democrats’ never-before-used process of voting on a new nominee involved hundreds of Democratic delegates gathering in Bangor, about 209 kilometres north of Portland. The delegates were elected at county party meetings last weekend, and Jackson scored an easy victory over just one opponent.
He first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat inside Maine’s House of Representatives. He lost, but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004, and eventually became the Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024.
He came in third while running for governor in this year’s Democratic primary, but had the backing of Platner and Our Revolution, the political organization founded by Sanders. Once Platner dropped out on July 10, a flood of former governor candidates – including Jackson – jumped to try to take his place. But by July 19, most had abandoned their bids, with Jackson emerging as the clear favourite.
Jackson received early support from progressives who had backed Platner before he dropped out. Our Revolution initially backed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate. When Platner left the race, the group rallied behind Jackson.
He has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He also has called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month.
Jackson acknowledged the disappointment of Platner’s supporters and the need to win them over for the general election.
“I agree there are people that are still very frustrated and angry what happened. I understand that,” he said to reporters. “All I’m trying to do is explain to them that his campaign was about the issues.”

“But concern does not lower the costs of groceries or gas. Concern does not keep our monitoring wards of rural hospitals like down in Lincoln County open. Concern does not restore all the rights that she’s taken away,” Jackson continued.

The Collins campaign criticized Jackson’s candidacy as “low-energy” and the product of a closed process run by Democratic Party elites.
“Today, in a process concocted by the Maine Democratic Party establishment, a 24-year Augusta insider was appointed to run for the Senate by fewer than three-tenths of one percent of its primary voters,” Collins campaign spokesman Shawn Roderick said in a statement, adding: “Our campaign will continue to run on Senator Collins’ bipartisan record of delivering results for Maine and America, which will stand in stark contrast to Troy’s low-energy campaign and his partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state.”
As his focus turns to Collins, Jackson must confront several daunting tasks, and with no time to spare.
He has to not only build a statewide campaign. He has to raise millions of dollars to compete on the airwaves.
Most of all, he has to convince huge numbers of Mainers who have repeatedly backed Collins for decades that it’s time for her to go.
Jackson’s path to victory
Many Democrats backed Jackson’s bid because they saw him as the candidate with the best chance of defeating Collins in November.
Supporters of Jackson, a former logger and longtime legislator from Allagash, a tiny town at the northern tip of the state, believe he will have unique appeal to working-class voters and cut into Collins’ margins in rural Maine. It’s the first time Collins, from Aroostook County, will be facing an opponent who also hails from the same sprawling area.
“The working class has been left behind and forgotten about,” said Shelly Mountain, a former Aroostook County Democratic Committee chairwoman and a pro-Jackson delegate at the convention.
“He is definitely working class and always — has always,” she emphasized again, “been a champion for the working class.”
A Democratic strategist with experience in Maine races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race and Jackson’s potential challenges, noted that a Democratic statewide win against Collins involves narrowing a likely loss in the rural 2nd Congressional District to high single digits.
“Being from Aroostook County and having shown a pretty significant overperformance in his state Senate races, [Jackson] is well-suited to do that,” the strategist said, later adding: “Of course, Sen. Collins is not a pushover. She’s done very well over the state but also particularly the 2nd District.”
Other Democrats noted that Jackson mainly has to run up the score in traditionally Democratic strongholds of Portland and other cities.
“There’s a path without expanding the map,” said David Farmer, a Maine Democratic strategist. He noted that Collins’ 2020 opponent, former state House Speaker Sara Gideon, underperformed the Democratic presidential ticket in Portland and other blue areas, due in part to a third-party candidate.
Farmer was optimistic that this year, Democrats would stay united.
“The reactions to Trump, to the ICE killing in Biddeford, to high prices, to the war [with Iran] — that solidifies Democrats so they’re less likely to drift than in 2020,” Farmer said.
But the Democratic strategist noted that when Jackson ran in the party’s primary for governor earlier this year, he struggled in more affluent parts of the state where Collins has performed well, even as they have shifted away from the GOP in the Trump era.
“He’ll need to do better in the greater Portland suburbs,” the strategist said.
The 2020 election provides some clues about Jackson’s challenges ahead. That year, Collins won re-election nearly 9 points even as Joe Biden carried the state by the same margin.
Exit polls show that Collins overperformed with independents, moderates and women. Independents who voted for Biden by 24 points also voted for Collins by 3 points. Self-identified moderates swung 24 points for Biden, but they voted for Collins by 7 points.
Women, who have long been key to Collins’ victories, broke for Biden by 23 points, but they voted for Collins by 3 points. Collins overperformed among women who didn’t go to college and limited the margin of defeat among white women with college degrees, one of Democrats’ strongest constituencies.
More challenges ahead
Jackson’s most immediate challenge is fundraising. His campaign announced Wednesday that it had raised over $600,000 in roughly 72 hours, surpassing $1 million since launching his Senate run on July 8. Collins’ campaign had $11 million to spend as of June 30, and Republican groups are gearing up to spend millions more.
Asked if he has enough money to win the race, Jackson said with a laugh, “Well not now, but I hope to get it,” adding that he’ll have the resources to prevail “because we got the right message.”
Jackson is likely to get outside help, too, as Democratic groups that had abandoned Platner amid his scandals re-engage in the race.
Ahead of the convention, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, signaled that Jackson could expect full support from the deep-pocketed party apparatus once he clinched the nomination.
“We’re excited for Maine,” Gillibrand said, adding that after state Democrats “finish their primary,” the DSCC will “support whoever wins.”
Jackson said Saturday that he has not spoken with any Democratic senators, and had not yet spoken with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Republicans, meanwhile, are gearing up to unload attacks on Jackson, particularly over his long tenure in the state Legislature and his ties to Platner.
Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP super PAC, is launching a new six-figure ad campaign aimed at Jackson, starting with a digital ad launching on Saturday. The group has plans to spend more than $42 million on the race.
The ad highlights recent headlines on Jackson’s temper and heated confrontations with legislative colleagues, with a narrator saying, “A volatile personality, anger issues with women, verbal abuse. It’s not Graham Platner, it’s Troy Jackson. Jackson has a history of conflicts with women, bullying, even intimidation.”
“I disagree,” Jackson said when asked about the ad after the convention on Saturday.
“I am passionate about those issues. I mean, there’s just no doubt about it,” Jackson said, later adding: “Anyone that I may have argued with, that I might have went too far or got too passionate. I apologize to. But I don’t have a problem with anyone in the Legislature and the U.S. Senate.”
Jackson’s supporters were not concerned about those attacks.
“If I had been going through the same bulls--- argument about stripping people’s coverage for their medications, I’d be throwing f-----g water bottles too,” said McGinley Jones, a 56-year-old small-business owner and convention delegate from Washington County, referring to an episode where Jackson reportedly threw a water bottle during a meeting on prescription drug legislation.
“I’m all for him getting passionate,” said Jim Gerritsen, an organic farmer representing Aroostook County at the convention, who has worked with Jackson on some pieces of legislation. “I’m all for him getting strong to fight for us because we know for sure that Susan Collins has never lifted a finger in her life to fight for the working class.”
Jackson and Platner were close allies and campaigned together, although Jackson quickly called on Platner to step aside following the sexual assault allegation.
Lance Dutson, a GOP strategist in Maine who worked on Collins’ past campaigns but is not involved in the race, suggested the contest resets without Platner, whose viral videos and impassioned critiques of the political and economic systems catapulted him to national fame.
With a “generic Democrat” as her opponent, Dutson predicted the contest would focus instead on their legislative records.
“People are going to be able to put his record up against Collins’ record. And there’s really no comparison between the two,” Dutson said, noting that Collins can point to “literally billions and billions of dollars” she has brought to Maine as a longtime member, and now chairwoman, of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.
Collins herself has already started to try and define Jackson as out of step with Mainers.
She told NBC News earlier this week that Jackson “seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” and she recently told CNN that Jackson is a “Bernie bro,” referring to his support for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., during the 2016 presidential primary.
Sanders, who endorsed both Jackson and Platner in their primaries, stayed out of the brief race to pick a new Senate nominee. But he praised Jackson this week as someone who “understands the problems of the working class in Maine and throughout this country.”
Dutson, the GOP consultant, acknowledged that Jackson could have some appeal in rural parts of the state given his roots in northern Maine, but said his policies were still too far left.
“If you’re from Aroostook County, Maine, but you’re standing onstage with Bernie Sanders, that’s just a massive disconnect,” Dutson said.
One reason Democrats are relieved is Jackson wins them back voters like Carol Eisenberg, a lawyer based in Maine, who supported Janet Mills in the primary and was leery of Platner after he won the nomination.
Jackson “has my full support,” she said. “I would never cast a ballot for Susan Collins. I just wasn’t sure if I would be able to cast one for Platner.”
