sources.text:
Troy Jackson officially clinches Maine Democratic U.S. Senate nomination
Troy Jackson speaks to delegates ahead of becoming the official Democratic U.S. Senate nominee at the convention in Bangor on July 25, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Former logger from Allagash turned politician Troy Jackson on Saturday officially became the Democratic nominee in the U.S. Senate race for longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ seat.
All but one of Jackson’s opponents had suspended their campaigns over the past week, resulting in a largely ceremonious convention to replace former nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out following an accusation of sexual assault earlier this month.
“We are not from the left. We are not from the right. We’re from the bottom, and we are rising,” Jackson said in his acceptance speech, echoing Platner’s stump speech against the wealthy’s hold on the political system that had energized voters across the state.
Jackson’s domination of the quasi-improvised process that the Maine Democratic Party raced to pull together in the days after Platner’s late exit was on full display Saturday, as Jackson secured the votes of 566 delegates, many of whom began chanting “Troy” before voting began.
The only other candidate who remained in the race, Saundra Pelletier, CEO of Evofem Biosciences Inc., a woman’s pharmaceutical company, received just five votes, but used her speech to underscore that the party’s rules gave delegates free rein to back whoever they wanted Saturday.
Speaking with Maine Morning Star ahead of Saturday’s program, Pelletier said she knew she was “swinging for the fences,” but could not bypass an opportunity to get into the fight to oust Collins. Now, she plans to continue to stay involved in whatever way she can.
“I’d do anything asked of me to help, except walking nude down the street,” Pelletier told Maine Morning Star.
While 13 people had launched campaigns to replace Platner, that list significantly shrank as it became clear last weekend that the delegates each county selected to send to the nominating convention were overwhelmingly supporters of Jackson.
Of the 601 delegates, 101 were members of the state committee and 500 were elected proportionally by county committees. Ahead of the county caucuses to pick those representatives, Jackson and other campaigns worked quickly to line up slates of supportive delegates to increase their odds of securing the nomination.
While not obligated to vote for him, 95% of the county delegates chosen were already aligned with Jackson heading into the convention, demonstrating the organizing prowess of his campaign just off of his June 9 loss in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, where he came in third.
Momentum behind Jackson’s campaign was also underscored earlier this week by the more than $1 million his campaign says it has raised since launching his Senate bid. However, it is still a far cry from the $11 million cash on hand Collins reported, as of the last filing deadline.
What energized delegates
Sporting a Platner t-shirt, Zachary Shomler, who had volunteered for the oyster farmer’s campaign, became a delegate “to continue the work we started,” he said.
The Democrat from Calais had never previously volunteered for a campaign but after seeing Platner’s launch video last August immediately contacted his team. While the charismatic video drew him in, it was Platner’s detailed policy plans — which Shomler described as “a list of every grievance I have with our country” — that kept him in the fight.
From knocking doors in Washington County, Shomler has become well acquainted with the unique challenges of energizing Democratic and independent voters in Maine’s small towns, where doing business is dependent on having good relationships.
With limited time heading into the general election, Shomler hopes to make use of the volunteer infrastructure he helped build in Washington County to help Jackson, who he’d voted for as his first choice in the Democratic primary for governor.
Jackson, who had campaigned alongside Platner, holds many of the same progressive policy stances as the former nominee, including Medicare for all, abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and fighting back against the wealthy’s hold on the political system, to name a few. He reiterated these views during both his speech to delegates ahead of the vote and after results were announced on Saturday, before turning to critiques of Collins.
“Concern does not lower the cost of groceries or gas,” Jackson said, a nod to the oft-repeated critique of Collins being “concerned” about issues but not casting votes to rectify them.
Saturday was the second time Michael Leconte of Portland served as a party delegate, the first being during one of independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont’s bids for president. Sanders’ bid had also been the first time Leconte, who identifies as a Democratic socialist, became invested in electoral politics.
The 41-year-old had been hesitant about backing Platner as a candidate, and abstained from voting in the primary, but fully supported his policies.
“You don’t follow after a demagogue,” Leconte said. “You let those ideals be championed by whoever is willing to step up and do it. So it was Platner, now it’s Jackson.”
Far more Mainers than were permitted had wanted to be a part of the convention, as 3,700 Democratic voters competed for the 500 spots. Independent voters — who have historically been consequential in Maine elections and were able to vote in the semi-open primary in which Platner had been selected — were not allowed to participate.
Some of the Mainers not selected as delegates still volunteered their time Saturday, including David Statman of Rockland, who said he feels the high number of people who have wanted to be a part of the process demonstrates that “the party is really coming together.”
Other Mainers attended as guests to observe the unprecedented proceedings, including Democratic U.S. House nominee and state treasurer Matt Dunlap.
Amy Fried, an alternate for Penobscot County, was one of few delegates who hadn’t vowed to support any particular candidate in advance, though said ahead of voting Saturday, “I don’t plan to support people with no experience,” which had been a concern she’d had with Platner, too.
That’s been a tension in this race, a key contrast between Platner and Gov. Janet Mills when she’d been in the running. While Platner was a political newcomer plucked by activists to launch a bid, Jackson has nearly two decades of experience working in state politics.
Morgan Urquhart of Bangor has been witness to that first hand, having worked for Jackson when he was president of the Maine Senate.
With her 10-year-old daughter in tow Saturday, Urquhart said she had voted for Platner in the primary but, similar to many delegates, said that for her it was never about one candidate.
“People are ready for change,” Urquhart said. “For me, I think that’s what a lot of the excitement in the primary was about. Troy’s been in the same fight for a long time.”
Jackson’s track record
During Jackon’s time as a legislator, his political views have publicly evolved. Jackson first unsuccessfully ran for his local state House of Representatives seat in 2000 as a Republican, before winning as an independent in 2002. He joined the Democratic Party in 2004.
As a legislator, Jackson voted against marriage equality in 2009 and for several anti-abortion measures through 2013 (though he told Maine Public in 2022 he continued to struggle with abortion).
But as president of the Maine Senate from 2018 to 2024, when he termed out, Jackson voted for several bills to expand abortion access — earning 100% ratings from Planned Parenthood’s Maine chapter and the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Maine.
His shifting views on abortion were already the focus of opposition ads during his bid for governor this year.
As a legislator, Jackson also championed bills to reduce drug prices, expand child care, provide free school meals and strengthen labor standards, including providing loggers and haulers the right to bargain together, among others. He has also claimed to hold the state record for most bills vetoed, which he touts as evidence of fighting for progressive policies despite pushback.
Though Jackson first ran for office in 2000, he traces his political start to a 1998 border blockade, an origin story he’s often repeated, including while rallying alongside Platner as a gubernatorial candidate.
In protest of timber landowners bypassing local workers to hire cheaper temporary Canadian labor, Jackson led a week-long blockade in northern Maine. The standoff ended with Jackson and others being escorted away by police.
“I didn’t get involved in politics because I wanted the title,” Jackson before recounting that story again Saturday. “I got involved because the people that I worked beside were getting screwed, and nobody, no one in power, seemed to care.”
With 101 days before the November election, Maine Democratic Party Chair Charlie Dingman urged attendees to exit the convention carrying “the fantastic energy in this room and the imagination that brought us all here together, determined to protect our beautiful state and its people.”

Maine Democrats pick Troy Jackson to replace Platner as Senate nominee
Former state Senate president will take on longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins
BANGOR, Maine – With just over 100 days to go until the midterm elections, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson officially clinched the Democratic nomination for Senate at a party convention here Saturday, setting up a marquee fall matchup against longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Jackson will replace Graham Platner, who withdrew as the nominee just over two weeks ago after an allegation of sexual assault, which he denies.
“This process came together faster than any of us expected,” Jackson said in his victory speech before the gathered delegates and party officials at the Cross Insurance Center. “But this is important. The movement represented in this room did not just begin two weeks ago.”
Delegates picked Jackson over pharmaceutical executive Saundra Pelletier by a vote of 566-5 during a roughly two-and-a-half hour party convention that also served as a fall campaign kickoff for the state’s Democratic faithful.
“Power is never just given to working people. We have to band together and take it,” Jackson said earlier Saturday during his nominating address. “When the people in power refuse to listen, well, you have to organize. You have to stand together in solidarity together.”
“That’s how we took on the companies exploiting Maine loggers, and it’s how we’re going to take on Susan Collins,” he said.
Jackson’s pick wraps up a chaotic few weeks for Maine Democrats, who had to convene Saturday’s convention to pick a new nominee ahead of a Monday deadline. They’ve been seeking to move on from Platner, who easily defeated Gov. Janet Mills in a primary last month with a populist message that resonated with Democratic voters despite a series of negative headlines that dogged his nearly yearlong campaign.
Jackson, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, came into the convention as the prohibitive favorite after securing the support of a vast majority of delegates elected across the state’s counties last weekend to serve at the convention.
Eve Breedlove, a young delegate from Penobscot County, said she’d supported Jackson in the gubernatorial race because of his support for progressive policies, which she said were similar to what Platner had campaigned on.
“People still had that momentum behind him, and just with all of this happening, it’s unprecedented,” she said. “But in a way, I’m only 20 years old, so everything that’s ever happened in my life is very unprecedented.”
Now, Democrats are looking ahead to November, when ousting Collins, the only Senate Republican to represent a seat carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, will be critical to their chances of flipping the chamber. Democratic delegates — many of whom said they’d known Jackson for years — called the new nominee an authentic candidate who would be a strong challenger to Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in the blue-leaning state.
“It’s going to be tough, but he’s got a real passionate support base,” said Melissa Smith, a Waldo County delegate who said she’d known Jackson for a decade. “People are tired of Susan Collins. She hasn’t done a town hall in what, 25, 30 years? The only way you can talk to Susan Collins is if you happen to run into her at the Hannaford [grocery store].”
A longtime state legislator, Jackson rose to serve as state Senate president for six years, leaving the role in 2024 due to term limits. A logger from northern Maine, his electoral career began in 2000, when he lost a race for the state House as a Republican before winning the seat as an independent two years later.
In 2004, he joined the Democratic Party and went on to serve in the state Senate from 2008 until 2014, when he left for an unsuccessful bid for Maine’s 2nd District. He returned to the chamber in 2016 for what would be an eight-year stint.
Jackson finished in third place last month in Maine’s ranked choice Democratic primary for governor.
His top competitors from that race, including Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and former state public health official Nirav Shah, revived their campaigns this month to seek the Senate nomination but dropped out last weekend after Jackson’s campaign said a majority of the delegates had pledged to support him.
Jordan Wood, who lost the Democratic primary for the open 2nd District, and Dan Kleban, a founder of Maine Beer Company who briefly ran for Senate last year before endorsing Mills, were also among the candidates who entered the snap Senate primary before ending their campaigns and rallying around Jackson.
Pelletier was the only other candidate who remained in the race through Saturday.
Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee to succeed retiring Rep. Jared Golden in the 2nd District, said Democrats running across the state were all focused on the issues motivating Maine voters.
“What you’re seeing here is that that groundswell of energy that was really inspired by Platner’s campaign was really inspired by the same priorities that we’ve all been putting forward,” he said in an interview Saturday.
In his remarks on Saturday morning, Jackson touted health care, union rights and a living wage for workers as top priorities. He also stressed his support for reproductive and LGBTQ rights, two key Democratic issues on which he held more conservative positions earlier in his career.
He won big cheers in the convention hall Saturday as he spoke about his support for unions, which were critical in helping elect pro-Jackson delegates at the nominating meetings last weekend.
Fall matchup
Democrats looking to flip the Senate — a prospect that looked unlikely a year ago — have expanded the map into red-leaning states ahead of the fall campaign, but Maine remains a top target.
While national groups briefly appeared ready to step back from the race before Platner’s withdrawal, party leaders immediately endorsed Jackson on Saturday after publicly opting for a hands-off approach during the past few weeks.
Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand said Jackson had a “demonstrated ability to win.”
“A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been,” the two New Yorkers said in a joint statement.
Jackson told reporters on Saturday that he had not yet spoken with Schumer.
He enters the general election with a significant cash disparity against Collins, whose campaign ended June with $11 million on hand, according to her second-quarter federal filings. Jackson said he expected to have the resources to win “because we’ve got the right message.”
Affordable Maine, a Democratic advocacy group, on Friday released two new ads attacking Collins, one focused on a congressional stock trading ban and another on her vote to confirm Brett M. Kavanaugh, who was among the Supreme Court justices who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022.
But Republicans appear ready to try to tie Jackson to Platner, and to highlight reports of his hot temper while serving in the state legislature. On Saturday, Republicans called him a “Democratic socialist” and an “ineffective legislator.”
“Troy Jackson lost his bid to be governor and he will lose his bid to be senator. Jackson is a Democrat socialist who has only made life harder in Maine, while Susan Collins has secured $1.5 billion in funding to benefit Mainers in all 16 counties,” Samantha Cantrell, a National Republican Senatorial Committee regional press secretary, said in a statement.
Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC with ties to the chamber’s GOP leaders, launched a six-figure ad campaign Saturday focused on the reports about Jackson’s temperament as part of the $42 million the group has pledged to spend in Maine this year.
“Chuck Schumer forcefully removed Graham Platner from the ballot against the will of Maine voters, only to replace him with a deranged and scandal-plagued political insider,” SLF spokesman Chris Gustafson said in a statement.
Jackson said Saturday that he anticipated the Republican attacks while acknowledging that he’d fought with people from both parties while in the legislature.
“I’ve cried on the Senate floor because I believe that people sent me to Augusta to deliver for them, and it’s important to me,” he told reporters. “Anyone that I may have argued with, that I might have went too far and got too passionate, I apologize to. But I don’t have a problem with anyone in the legislature or in the U.S. Senate.”
Other Democrats sought to more subtly address those concerns. Charlotte Warren, a former mayor of Hallowell and onetime state legislator who reportedly clashed with Jackson in 2021, said he “wears his heart on his sleeve” as she formally nominated him at the convention.
“What I’ve learned about Troy in these moments: He listens. He works through disagreements, and when the fight is over he gets back to work for what he believes in, with the people he believes in,” she said.

It takes a lot for a Democrat to have enough skeletons in his closet for other Democrats to turn on him.

sources.news_title: Troy Jackson wins the Democratic nomination to challenge Sen. Susan Collins
sources.text:
Troy Jackson won the Democratic nomination for Maine’s U.S. Senate seat on Saturday, capping nearly three weeks of political drama following the collapse of Graham Platner’s populist campaign.
Hundreds of Democratic delegates from across Maine chose Jackson — a logger and former Maine Senate president — to take on Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins this fall in a pivotal race that both parties regard as key to control of the Senate. Jackson faced only one opponent, Saundra Pelletier, during Saturday’s nominating convention in Bangor because all of his better-known rivals withdrew after his supporters dominated last weekend’s delegate-selection process.
Jackson received 566 votes versus five votes for Pelletier, a biopharmaceutical executive running for public office for the first time.
"Are you ready to defeat Susan Collins?" Jackson said prior to the vote, prompting a roar of approval from the nearly 600 delegates. "Well then let's unite this party, let's build the largest working-class movement Maine has ever seen and let's win this thing."
Collins is widely viewed as especially vulnerable this year as the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state won by Democrat Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election. Polls suggest that President Donald Trump and his policies are unpopular with the independents who make up a third of Maine's electorate and who have often been key to Collins' longevity in Congress.
But Collins has used her position as chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee to bring hundreds of millions of dollars back to Maine. The Collins campaign has portrayed her as a steady leader and moderate dealmaker in bitterly divided DC.
Her campaign and its Republican allies immediately sought to cast Jackson as a "socialist" or a "far-left" candidate chosen by Democratic insiders.
"Troy Jackson will attempt to sell Mainers a multi-trillion-dollar bill of goods based on rhetoric that will make everything sound free, but in reality would be paid for by middle- and lower-income workers," Shawn Roderick, spokesman for the Collins campaign, said in a statement. “Our campaign will continue to run on Senator Collins’ bipartisan record of delivering results for Maine and America, which will stand in stark contrast to Troy’s low-energy campaign and his partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state."
From logger to Senate contender
It was a remarkable turn of events for Jackson, a blue-collar progressive who says just one month ago he was fishing the remote waters near his hometown in Allagash after finishing third in the Democratic primary for governor.
Then Platner withdrew from the Senate race after an ex-romantic partner leveled allegations of rape against him in a story published by POLITICO. Platner denied the allegations. But Jackson, who had campaigned with Platner several times, successfully positioned himself as the best person to continue pushing the issues that had drawn so many frustrated Democrats and independents to the former nominee's campaign.
Jackson pledged to work toward universal health care, to defend workers' rights and reproductive rights, and to stand up to the Trump administration and to what he says is a "billionaire class" that is getting wealthier and wealthier on the backs of lower- and middle-class Americans.
"We will welcome Democrats, independents and Republicans who believe that working people, working people, finally deserve a fair deal," Jackson said in his post-nomination speech. "Even when we don't agree on every issue because this movement is not from the left, it is not from the right. It's from the bottom, and we are rising."
A fifth-generation logger, Jackson represented far northern Maine for 20 years in the Maine House and Senate, winning term after term as a Democrat even as the region turned increasingly Republican. He served as Senate president for six of those years.
Jackson got his start in politics after helping to lead a blockade of logging road border crossings in 1998 to protest landowners’ hiring lower-paid Canadian loggers to work in the Maine woods. He has been heavily involved with Maine’s labor unions — and that support appeared to have been critical in his ability to organize supporters to run for delegates and then vote in last week’s process.
Democrats' three-week sprint
Maine Democratic Party leaders had less than three weeks under state law to select a new nominee after Platner withdrew. Facing intense pressure to respect the massive grassroots support behind Platner, party leaders settled on county-by-county, caucus-style meetings to elect delegates to the nominating convention held on Saturday.
There were 12 declared candidates headed into last weekend’s delegate-selection process. Three of those candidates — Jackson, Nirav Shah and Shenna Bellows — ran in last month’s gubernatorial primary, as did former 2nd Congressional District candidate Jordan Wood.
But as the first county results began coming in, it quickly became clear that nearly all of the delegate spots were being filled by Jackson supporters. Jackson was able to tap into his strong support among union members as well as Platner’s massive volunteer network to turn out large numbers across the state.
By the end of the the second day of voting, all of Jackson’s top rivals had withdrawn from the race, clearing the path for Jackson’s official nomination six days later.
The sole remaining challenger by Saturday was Pelletier who, like Jackson and Collins, grew up in Aroostook County before attending Husson College and building a successful career. She now serves as CEO of Evofem Biosciences, a biopharmaceutical company that produces prescription drugs related to female reproductive health.
During her speech to delegates before Saturday's vote, Pelletier said she has "spent my career shaming the powerful" and pledged to be calm, measured leader "with the heart, the head and the backbone to know how to negotiate." She also cast herself as the best person to win the moderates and independents needed to defeat Collins.
"[Collins] is going to try to run the same campaign that she has always run," Pelletier said. "We have a chance to stop her. Today is an opportunity for you to select a candidate that can beat Susan Collins. It is time that we have a Democrat in that seat."
The response from the delegates was polite and respectful. But it paled in comparison to the reception and standing ovations that Jackson received during the two times he addressed the crowd on Saturday, sometimes fighting back his emotions as he recalled his upbringing in a logging family and years spent working in the woods.
But Jackson also seemed to acknowledge the deep divisions — even fissures — within the Democratic Party that were arguably best represented by Platner's meteoric rise to political fame. Platner received the largest number of primary votes in a Senate race in Maine history and drove Gov. Janet Mills — the candidate supported by national Democratic leaders — out of the race as he pledged to stand up to the political establishment.
"I've always known this,¹ that your trust has to be earned, and and so I want you to hear this directly from me: there is a place in this campaign for all of you," Jackson said. "There is work for you in this movement, and I will spend every day now through November earning that trust, because today we turn the page. Today this becomes a general election campaign."
Late entrance into high-stakes race
Jackson now faces the daunting task of quickly ramping up a campaign against Collins, a 30-year Senate veteran who has handily defeated every opponent in her four previous re-election campaigns. He also enters that campaign at a financial and organizational disadvantage with only 3 1/2 months left before Election Day. Republicans have already spent tens of millions of dollars to support Collins or to attack any potential challenger.
The political ad-tracking firm AdImpact has estimated that nearly $500 million will be spent on elections in Maine this year, with the Senate race consuming about $400 million of that figure. Much of that will be spent by the national parties and their deep-pocketed allies running PACs, super PACs and interest groups.
The Collins campaign, meanwhile, reported this week that it had raised $5.7 million during the last quarter and was sitting on $11 million in cash on hand.
"Troy Jackson is a Platner apologist, a radical Bernie Bro, and a walking red flag displaying all the warning signs of the early days of the Platner campaign," Kristen Cianci, spokesperson for the Republican National Committee. "Senator Susan Collins is a proven leader with unimpeachable character who will continue to deliver for Mainers when they re-elect her this November."
But Jackson reported raising more than $1 million during the first several weeks of his campaign and is expected to inherit a hefty sum raised by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — the campaign arm of the Senate Democratic caucus — for the eventual nominee.
"Troy Jackson is a fifth-generation logger with a demonstrated ability to win," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and DSCC chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said in a joint statement. "A champion of affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been."

sources.text:
Former state lawmaker and logger Troy Jackson secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine on Saturday.
He will face longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in November in a race that could decide which party controls the Senate.
Jackson replaces Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary in June but withdrew from the race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault that Platner has denied.

Platner’s exit forced Democrats to quickly come up with a never-before-used process to choose a new nominee, which involved more than 600 delegates from across the state gathering in Bangor. Jackson won the support of a majority of delegates to clinch the nomination.
Jackson’s victory was largely expected after his campaign touted that more than 480 delegates selected to go to the convention had promised to vote for him, a progressive who supports Medicare for All and dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Jackson first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat inside Maine’s House of Representatives. He lost, but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004, and eventually became the Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024.
He came in third while running for governor in this year’s Democratic primary election, but had the backing of Platner, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Our Revolution, the political organization founded by Sanders.
RELATED STORY | Bernie Sanders pulls support of Graham Platner after sexual assault allegation
Once Platner dropped out on July 10, a flood of former governor candidates — including Jackson — and others jumped to try to take Platner's place. But by July 19, most had abandoned their bids, with Jackson emerging as the clear favorite.
Jackson received early support from progressives who had backed Platner before he dropped out. Our Revolution, the political organization founded nearly a decade ago by Sen. Bernie Sanders, initially backed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate. When Platner left the race, the group rallied behind Jackson.
Jackson previously ran Maine operations for Sanders' 2016 presidential bid. This election cycle, Sanders endorsed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate, though the independent senator from Vermont withdrew his support for Platner after the sexual assault allegation. He said he didn't plan to weigh in on which Democrat should replace Platner.
Just one other candidate has remained in the race for the Senate nomination — women’s health company CEO Saundra Pelletier.
Jackson has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He also has called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month.
Maine is an important piece of Democrats’ effort to win the Senate
Democrats have a narrow path to take back the Senate in November and it’s highly unlikely they can do it without a win in Maine. In addition, they need victories in competitive races in North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, and they need to hang on to the seats they already have. That includes open Senate seats in Michigan and Minnesota, where Democratic incumbents are retiring.
Maine's Democratic primary was one of the early contests where progressives took on establishment-backed Democrats. While Platner faced several controversies during his campaign, he easily outlasted Gov. Janet Mills, who was backed by Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer but dropped out before the June 9 primary.
Platner had backing from Sanders as well as Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. That support disintegrated after the sexual assault allegation early this month.
Collins has described Jackson as a ‘Bernie Bro’
If he becomes the nominee, Jackson will need to convince the state's large independent voting bloc that it's time to replace Collins. Republicans have called Jackson too extreme for Maine voters, and Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are “clearly” in line with socialism.
She noted Jackson ran Sanders' first presidential campaign in Maine, adding “He's a Bernie Bro.”
Jackson would also need to scramble to make up a fundraising gulf against Collins, who has been raising money for months.
Federal filings show she has raised more than $16 million so far. Jackson's campaign this week said he raised more than $1 million since jumping into the Senate race.
Jackson said Saturday he believes his team is up to the task.
“We're not from the left, we're not from the right. We're from the bottom, and we are rising,” he said during a speech.

sources.news_title: Maine Democrats pick Troy Jackson as their Senate nominee at an unusual party convention
sources.text:
Bangor, Maine (CNN) — Maine Democrats picked Troy Jackson as their new Senate nominee on Saturday, the culmination of a brief and unusual contest that sets the stage for a 101-day sprint to try and defeat Republican Sen. Susan Collins in one of the country’s most important Senate races.
In a nearly unanimous vote, 566 delegates at a party convention in Bangor picked Jackson, the former state Senate president, as the nominee to replace Graham Platner after he dropped out earlier this month following an allegation of rape. Jackson faced little opposition at the convention after filling most delegate slots at county meetings with his supporters and forcing his most serious opponents to drop out.
After his overwhelming nomination, Jackson strode onto the stage to enthusiastic applause and booming strains of “Northern Attitude” by Noah Kahan, who grew up in nearby Vermont. In his acceptance speech, he zeroed in on a doubled-edged challenge: uniting Democrats and defeating Collins.
“There is a place in this campaign for all of you. There is work for you in this movement. And I will spend every day now through November earning that trust, because today we turn the page,” Jackson said. “Today, this becomes a general election campaign and today we begin the work of defeating Susan Collins in November.”
Democratic leaders in Washington, who stayed neutral in the nominating contest after a tense relationship with Platner, were quick to voice support for Jackson. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, head of the Senate Democratic campaign arm, dispatched aides to Maine to watch the process unfold and said in a statement that Jackson “has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat” Collins.
Republicans, meanwhile, made clear they plan to tie Jackson to Platner, who ended his campaign after an allegation of rape that he denied. Jackson was among those who called on Platner to drop out, but he previously aligned himself closely with the candidate.
Jackson pitched himself Saturday as a progressive working-class champion who could make the case that Collins has not stood up enough to President Donald Trump on behalf of Mainers. But he has work cut out for him against the incumbent, who has had a months-long head start in the race and proven to be a political survivor before.
Collins, who leads the Senate Appropriations Committee, has an extraordinary fundraising advantage. Her ads have played in heavy rotation for months, giving her a remarkable head start in the three-month sprint to November.
But during a fundraising event in Falmouth on Friday evening, Collins signaled to supporters that she is taking the race seriously. She has privately conceded that it could be her toughest campaign yet, given the political headwinds facing Republicans.
On Saturday, her campaign characterized Jackson’s nomination “an appointment” by a small group of Democratic voters while noting his unsuccessful bid for governor earlier this year.
“Our campaign will continue to run on Senator Collins’ bipartisan record of delivering results for Maine and America, which will stand in stark contrast to Troy’s low-energy campaign and his partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state,” campaign spokesperson Shawn Roderick said in a statement. “Just one month ago, Troy came in third in the Democratic primary for Governor. Now he will run for Senate as the third choice of his party insiders.”
Maine Democratic Party chairman Charles Dingman implored party activists to “buckle down for the next 100 days together.”
“Please carry with you the fantastic energy in this room and the imagination that brought us all here together,” he said, speaking as delegates applauded and waved “Retire Susan” signs in the air, a poignant nod to a key challenge for the party – making the race a referendum on Collins.
Jackson’s vision
Organizers of the party convention had envisioned a robust field of candidates vying to win a majority of the 601 delegates, 500 elected at the county level and 101 from the Democratic State Committee. Instead, Jackson entered the convention with only one opponent left: Saundra Pelletier, a CEO of a biopharmaceutical company who is a political unknown.
As a result, the nomination process on Saturday played out in an anticlimactic fashion, absent the drama that has loomed large over the Maine Democratic Party for weeks amid the scandal enveloping Platner. Jackson’s speech finished shortly before noon and delegates headed toward the doors – less than three hours after the convention began.
“We can’t allow six more years of the same thing,” Jackson said. “Let’s get to work winning this race.”
Maurie Hill, an alternate delegate to the special convention, said she believes dissatisfaction with Collins will help galvanize the party behind Jackson regardless of their initial preferences in the Senate contest.
“Our bottom line is making sure that Susan Collins doesn’t go back to the Senate,” Hill said, stopping for a moment to talk during a break in the proceedings. “More recently, I’m very distressed by her positions.”
Videos about Collins’ voting record and her 30 years in the Senate played on a loop on large screens at the convention, including one that showcased her long-ago pledge to serve no more than two terms. She is seeking her sixth – an about-face that she has defended because of how her Senate seniority benefits Maine.
“I was an infant when Susan Collins came into office,” said Elizabeth Ahlgren, a delegate from York, who noted that Collins and Jackson are both from Aroostook County in northern Maine, which could be an attribute for Democrats.
“It’s a region where she thinks she can always count on a base of support,” Ahlgren said. “Now we have someone who’s actually going to make her fight for them and earn those votes.”
While a far less polished orator than Platner, Jackson spoke with an air of authenticity about the challenges facing working Mainers.
“Susan Collins keeps telling us, `Everything is just fine.’ They act like we’re idiots. We know it isn’t,” Jackson said. “We all have eyes. We can see what’s happening. We can see our paychecks and the bills that we have. We know we are getting screwed and we also know who’s to blame and I’m running to change that.”
Jackson’s challenges
Fundraising will be one of Jackson’s most urgent priorities.
Collins’ campaign entered July with over $11 million cash on hand, while Jackson is effectively starting from scratch. His campaign has said he raised at least $1 million since launching his bid to replace Platner on the ballot.
Republicans are set to attack Jackson over his previous closeness to Platner and reports that have alleged angry outbursts with colleagues when he was a state lawmaker. Those reports were featured prominently in the debut ad against Jackson from the Senate Leaderhsip Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races.
Looking to blunt questions about his temperament, particularly around women, Jackson’s campaign selected former state Rep. Charlotte Warren to nominate him at the convention. She acknowledged they have not always agreed and are “very passionate people.”
“Yes, sometimes we fought one another,” Warren said to the crowd of convention delegates. “But here is what I’ve learned about Troy in these moments: He listens, he works through disagreements, and when the fight is over, he gets back to work for what he believes in, with the people he believes in.”
Pelletier did not directly criticize Jackson in a speech before the vote, but she said Maine Democrats need “a leader that’s measured, that’s calm, that knows how to behave under serious pressure.”
Jackson will also have to grapple with how much he embraced Platner earlier in the election cycle. He campaigned alongside him multiple times, stood by him through earlier scandals and was Platner’s top choice in the primary for governor.
Jackson did not mention Platner on Saturday but appealed to the Democrats that he energized in his campaign.
“I know many of you poured your hearts into building this movement way before I ever entered this race,” Jackson said in a speech before the vote. “The hope that you built never belonged to any one campaign.”

And despite recent reporting in The Washington Post and CNN describing Jackson as exhibiting a short temper with colleagues during his time in office, he has faced minimal public pushback from state leaders in the lead-up to the convention.
"He's passionate. He doesn't deviate. He's funny. He can get a little testy at times because he's passionate," said former state Sen. Susan Deschambault as she walked into the Cross Insurance Center where the convention was taking place Saturday. "That's what we need. We don't like what's going on now."
Whether Jackson can command the same level of enthusiasm that Platner garnered over the past year remains an open question, even to some Mainers who plan to cast their ballot for Jackson this fall.
Some Democrats contend that Platner and Jackson share the same set of values when it comes to the issues, arguing that is what will keep the momentum going for the party heading into the general election.
"Troy Jackson has been working at getting these progressive policies in Maine for years, like since before I was born," said 22-year-old delegate Kaia De Vries, a graduate student at the University of Maine. "It wasn't [Platner's] movement. This is a progressive movement that still exists, that will continue without him being a public-facing part of it."
Standing next to De Vries, 30-year-old Aurora Green agreed, saying no one individual is the face of this moment.
"This isn't about Graham Platner. This isn't even about Troy Jackson," she said. "This is about a movement of working-class Mainers and workers coming together and saying that we aren't going to be bought out and that we deserve better."
A tough road ahead for the nominee
While Collins has faced competitive challengers before, Democrats see the fifth-term incumbent as particularly vulnerable this year. She's running in a state carried by Kamala Harris in 2024, and at a moment when many voters have soured on President Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran.
Still, Jackson will face a difficult path to victory, with only about 100 days before voting ends on Nov. 3 to build up a war chest and make his case to voters.
In a statement for the Collins campaign, spokesperson Shawn Roderick criticized Jackson for what he described as a "partisan record of driving up costs, hurting our schools, and making life less affordable for families across the state."
"Senator Collins looks forward to waging a vigorous and issues-oriented campaign that will distinguish her record of accomplishment against Troy's angry sound bites and far-left ideology," the campaign said.
In Collins, Jackson is running against one of the most senior Republican incumbents in the Senate. Collins, who has held her seat for 30 years, holds a massive fundraising edge, reporting $11 million in cash on hand, according to latest Federal Election Commission filings.
But Jackson's campaign argues that it has momentum, reporting a fundraising haul of more than $1 million since he announced his run.
Jackson concluded his remarks Saturday with a call for unity.
"If you believe our freedoms are worth defending, stand with us. And if you believe that Maine deserves a senator who will fight like hell for working class people, well stand with us," he said. "We have a party to unite, we have a movement to build, and we have a senator to defeat, and together, we are going to win."

Maine Democratic delegates choose Troy Jackson as new nominee to face US Sen. Susan Collins
BANGOR, Maine (AP) — Former state lawmaker and logger Troy Jackson secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine on Saturday and will face longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in November in a race that could decide which party controls the chamber.
Jackson replaces Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary in June but withdrew from the race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault that Platner has denied. Maine Democrats met Saturday to choose a new Senate nominee to face Collins.
Support coalesced around Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and fifth-generation logger from rural northern Maine who campaigned alongside Platner during a failed bid for governor and was a favorite among progressives to replace him.
“When the people in power refuse to listen, you have to organize, you have to stand in solidarity, together. And you have to make them listen,” Jackson said during a speech at the last-minute nominating convention.
Democrats view Maine as the party’s best opportunity to flip a Senate seat this year because it’s a competitive race in a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024. But defeating Collins won’t be easy. The five-term incumbent holds a fundraising advantage, while Jackson will have less than four months to sell himself to voters.
Republicans immediately launched an ad campaign against Jackson, accusing him of having a volatile temper and linking him to Platner. The Senate Leadership Fund, Republicans’ super PAC, said it is committed to spending over $42 million against Jackson.
Collins has described Jackson as a ‘Bernie Bro’
Jackson, 58, will need to convince the state’s large independent voting bloc that it’s time to replace Collins, 73. Republicans have called Jackson too extreme for Maine voters, and Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are “clearly” in line with socialism.
“Troy Jackson will attempt to sell Mainers a multi-trillion dollar bill of goods based on rhetoric that will make everything sound free, but in reality would be paid for by middle and lower income workers,” said Collins’ campaign spokesperson, Shawn Roderick.
Both Jackson and Collins are from northern Maine, where traditional industries such as potato farming and timber harvesting are vital parts of the economy. Both will make the case over the next few months that they are the right leader to protect those industries, along with lobster fishing and tourism.
Collins noted that Jackson ran U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ first presidential campaign in Maine, adding “He’s a Bernie Bro.”
Asked by reporters about that description, Jackson said, “I don’t really care. What I am is a guy from northern Maine that’s a logger.”
He said he would attack Collins on what he described as her record of supporting tax cuts for the wealthy and failing to protect health care.
Jackson needs to scramble to make up a fundraising gulf against the incumbent, who has been raising money for months. Federal filings show she has raised more than $16 million so far. Jackson’s campaign this week said he raised more than $1 million since jumping into the Senate race.
Maine is an important piece of Democrats’ effort to win the Senate
Democrats have a narrow path to take back the Senate in November and it’s highly unlikely they can do it without a win in Maine. In addition, they need victories in competitive races in North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, and they need to hang on to the seats they already have. That includes open Senate seats in Michigan and Minnesota, where Democratic incumbents are retiring.
Maine’s Democratic primary was one of the early contests where progressives took on establishment-backed Democrats. While Platner faced several controversies during his campaign, he easily outlasted Gov. Janet Mills, who was backed by Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer but dropped out before the June 9 primary.
Platner had backing from Sanders as well as Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. That support disintegrated after the sexual assault allegation early this month.
Republicans began making the case Saturday that Jackson is too close to Platner. Jackson is “a Platner apologist, a radical Bernie Bro, and a walking red flag displaying all the warning signs of the early days of the Platner campaign,” RNC spokesperson Kristen Cianci said in a statement.
Jackson told reporters Saturday that he has not been in touch with Platner and is building a new movement. He didn’t mention Platner from the stage during his two addresses to Democratic delegates on Saturday, but said the campaign was “bigger than any one person.”
Jackson overwhelmingly won delegates’ support
The Maine Democratic Party scrambled to choose a new nominee after Platner, who sailed to victory in the Democratic primary in June, was accused by a former girlfriend of sexually assaulting her in 2021. Platner denies the allegation, but quit the race after key supporters called on him to withdraw.
Maine law gave the state party authority to choose a replacement and required a new nominee to be named by Monday — 101 days before the Nov. 3 election.
Maine Democrats’ never-before-used process of voting on a new nominee involved hundreds of Democratic delegates gathering in Bangor, about 130 miles (209 kilometers) north of Portland. The delegates were elected at county party meetings last weekend, and Jackson scored an easy victory over just one opponent.
He first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat inside Maine’s House of Representatives. He lost, but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004, and eventually became the Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024.
He came in third while running for governor in this year’s Democratic primary, but had the backing of Platner and Our Revolution, the political organization founded by Sanders. Once Platner dropped out on July 10, a flood of former governor candidates — including Jackson — jumped to try to take his place. But by July 19, most had abandoned their bids, with Jackson emerging as the clear favorite.
Jackson received early support from progressives who had backed Platner before he dropped out. Our Revolution initially backed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate. When Platner left the race, the group rallied behind Jackson.
He has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He also has called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month.
Jackson acknowledged the disappointment of Platner’s supporters and the need to win them over for the general election.
“I agree there are people that are still very frustrated and angry what happened. I understand that,” he said to reporters. “All I’m trying to do is explain to them that his campaign was about the issues.”
___
Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti and video journalist Nathan Ellgren in Washington contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Democrats pick new US Senate candidate after scandal
sources.text:
The Democratic Party in Maine picked its new candidate for a key US Senate race on Saturday, after the original nominee was pressured to drop out over sexual misconduct allegations.
Delegates to a hastily organised nominating convention picked Troy Jackson, a former state senate president, to go up against Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
"Thank you, Maine. In 101 days, we will defeat Susan Collins and reclaim our Senate seat. Let's get to work," Jackson wrote on X.
The move comes just over two weeks after the prior candidate, Graham Platner, dropped out.
A Marine veteran, oyster fisherman and political newcomer, Platner had earlier won the Democratic primary with an energetic, anti-establishment message that gained him national prominence.
He weathered earlier scandals, including one related to a Nazi-linked tattoo, but his support plummeted after a former partner publicly accused him of rape.
Platner, 41, strongly denied the allegation, but ultimately acceded to demands from across the party to drop out, just before a legal deadline allowing for a replacement.
Unlike Platner, 58-year-old Jackson has been in Maine politics for decades, beginning in the state House and ultimately becoming the top-ranked senator.
His nomination as the Democratic candidate for the US Senate comes despite his loss in the Democratic primary for governor.
A logger by trade, Jackson grew up on the border of French-speaking Canada.
"Troy Jackson is a fifth-generation logger with a demonstrated ability to win," top Democratic Senators Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand said in a statement.
"A champion for affordable health care and working people, Jackson has harnessed the grassroots energy in Maine and is well-positioned to defeat Susan Collins, who is more vulnerable than she has ever been."
Media coverage has highlighted Jackson's prior conservative stances, such as opposition to abortion, that he has since walked back.
Maine voted against President Donald Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024, making it one of the Democrats' prime targets to win back a majority in the narrowly divided US Senate. (AFP)
